summary:
Snapshot 2026-10-08 06:00 UTC. The Irkutsk oblast story is at its search peak. The Wikipedia "Plague (disease)" page is newly in the top 1000 at 22,231 views/day, and more than 60 mainstream pieces have run in 48 hours (NPR, CNN, BBC, AP, NYT, WaPo, Reuters, SciAm, MedPage). Most of the news is about the diplomatic and transparency fight. Plain, search-style answers about the disease itself are thinner, and that is where we can win.

Status, all dates checked. Oct 7 was a Wednesday. Russia acknowledged on Sunday Oct 4 that a 28-year-old institute employee had died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology". Russia told WHO it registered no plague case in Irkutsk oblast. Rospotrebnadzor reports no infections found among staff. About 189–200 people are under medical observation.
- On Oct 7, WHO's Tedros asked Russia to clarify media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause. WHO's Van Kerkhove said WHO does not know the causative agent.
- The same day, Kremlin spokesperson Peskov called most media reporting "false information".
- WHO has called the risk outside Russia "very low".
- CDC says there is "no indication of a broader threat to the United States" and is monitoring travellers. CDC is also quoted as calling the US risk "extremely low", with about 200 people a year travelling from the region to the US.
- There are no direct US–Russia commercial flights.

Plague is still "suspected" and not confirmed. Not confirmed is not ruled out.

Ranking logic: the playbook favours rising-stage plain questions, and both readings come from GLP-1 data only. Rising-stage Shorts had a median of 55 vs 26 for emerging. Named-subject question titles had a median of about 75 vs 4 for generic titles. So the top slots go to the questions people are typing now: the dated status / second-case decoder, "Is plague a risk in the US?", "Can it spread person to person?", "Is it curable?" and symptoms. Below them come the angles where news coverage is thin: how a case gets confirmed, why contacts are watched for weeks, lab containment, plague in US parks and pets, and vaccine status.

Two items are rejected: the bioweapon/weaponisation storyline (Trump and Rand Paul quotes) and "We should be terrified / it's worse" fear-bait. Re-check every status line against WHO, Rospotrebnadzor and CDC at publish time.

candidates.topic: Plague status decoder: reports of a second Irkutsk institute worker with pneumonia. WHO asked Russia to clarify on Oct 7; the Kremlin called most reporting 'false information'
candidates.angle: 'Irkutsk Plague Case: Is There a Second Case? What's Confirmed vs Reported (as of Oct 7)'. A 3-column card: Confirmed (one death from pneumonia of unknown cause, acknowledged Oct 4; about 189–200 people under observation), Reported (a second employee ill, per media outlets WHO cited), and Officially stated (Russia told WHO no plague case was registered; WHO says it does not know the causative agent). Key line: not confirmed is not ruled out. Every claim is credited to its named source.
candidates.why_now: WHO (Tedros, Van Kerkhove) and the Kremlin issued conflicting statements on Oct 7 about a possible second case. Al Jazeera, Euronews, NewsNation and the Washington Times are all running it, so people are searching for whether it is real. A dated decoder title matches our best format (decoder titles reached 150, 60 and 55).

evidence.signal: Oct 7 (Wed): Tedros urged Russia to clarify reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause; Peskov called most reporting false; Van Kerkhove said WHO doesn't know the causative agent
WHO seeks clarity on the suspected plague death and a possible second case
Running 'what we know' explainer

candidates.topic: Is the Russia plague report a risk in the US? CDC: 'no indication of a broader threat'; WHO: 'very low' risk outside Russia; no direct US–Russia flights
candidates.angle: 'Plague in Russia: Is the US at Risk? What CDC and WHO Actually Said'. Quote each agency's exact risk words with the date. Explain what CDC traveller monitoring involves and why it is standard practice. Add the calming facts: no direct commercial flights since 2022, and about 200 travellers a year come from the region (reported CDC figure). Close with the urgent-care line for anyone with possible exposure.
keywords: is plague coming to the us
should i be worried about plague
candidates.why_now: Axios reports the US is tracking Siberia travellers. NBC Chicago, SFGATE and TODAY ran 'should you be worried?' pieces. The US Embassy and State Department have issued notices. That is local-angle demand across the US audience, and an attributed answer is the calm version of what people are asking.

evidence.signal: CDC: no indication of a broader threat to the US; WHO: 'very low' risk outside Russia
No direct US–Russia commercial flights; no added US travel restrictions
CDC quoted calling US risk 'extremely low'; about 200 people a year travel from the region to the US

candidates.topic: Can pneumonic plague spread person to person? Close-contact respiratory droplets vs truly airborne viruses like measles and COVID
candidates.angle: 'Can Pneumonic Plague Spread Person to Person?' Answer in 10 seconds: yes, but only pneumonic plague, and it requires direct, close contact (use the source's verbs). Then compare it with measles, which hangs in room air, and explain why that makes contact tracing work. Add the CDC fact that there has been no US person-to-person spread since 1924.
keywords: can pneumonic plague spread person to person
candidates.why_now: Seen in 3 snapshots with steady momentum of 90–92. BBC ('Why a global outbreak is unlikely'), NPR and SciAm explainers are all driving the question. This is the most-searched mechanism question in the story.

evidence.signal: 'What is pneumonic plague and how does it spread?'
Only pneumonic plague spreads person to person, via droplets with close contact
Plague (disease): 22,231 views/day, new in top 1000

candidates.topic: Is plague curable? Antibiotics work when started early; untreated pneumonic plague is usually fatal
candidates.angle: 'Is Plague Curable With Antibiotics?' Yes: standard antibiotics treat it, and the clock matters most for pneumonic plague. Say why early treatment is the whole game. Do not name doses. Say that health authorities, not individuals, give preventive antibiotics to close contacts. End with the urgent-care line and a no-stockpiling message.
candidates.why_now: News coverage repeats 'treatable with antibiotics' without explaining the timing, and the 'no cure' myth is circulating. A plain question title matches our top formula.

evidence.signal: Explainers state pneumonic plague is treatable with antibiotics and unlikely to spread widely
Plague FAQ published Oct 5, 2026

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague symptoms and timing: fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain; incubation as short as about 1 day; when to get urgent care
candidates.angle: 'What Are the Symptoms of Pneumonic Plague?' Give CDC's full warning-sign list, the incubation window as WHO and CDC state it, and tie the red flags to possible exposure (travel to or contact with a known case, or handling sick wild animals in plague areas). Say plainly that an ordinary cough or cold is not plague. Then: contact a doctor or local health authority urgently.
keywords: how fast does pneumonic plague kill
candidates.why_now: Symptom searches rise with every headline. Mainstream pieces list symptoms but rarely give the exposure context that keeps people from panicking over a normal cough.

evidence.signal: Symptoms: fever, headache, weakness, rapid pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain, cough
Official pneumonic plague fact sheet

candidates.topic: Plague still occurs in the US: an average of 7 human cases a year (CDC), mostly bubonic, mostly in rural West; hikers, campers and national parks
candidates.angle: 'Plague in the US: CDC Counts About 7 Human Cases a Year. Here's Where and Why'. Cover the Southwest, Northern California and Oregon foci; give the range, not a fixed figure. Explain fleas and rodents, and practical prevention for hikers (don't feed squirrels, use repellent, keep pets flea-treated). Point out that most US cases are bubonic and not person-to-person. No 'near you' phrasing.
candidates.why_now: An AP piece, 'The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year', is syndicated across ABC, Boston Herald and others. Outside Magazine ran a hikers piece on Oct 7. US audiences are turning the story toward themselves.

evidence.signal: 'The plague never went away…US nearly every year' (Oct 8)
'The Plague Is Still in U.S. National Parks…What Hikers Need to Know' (Oct 7)
Hiker plague explainer citing CDC average of about 7 human cases a year

candidates.topic: Why about 200 people are being watched: how contact tracing, isolation, medical observation and preventive antibiotics stop pneumonic plague
candidates.angle: 'Possible Plague Exposure? What Health Authorities Do Next'. Explain why 'under observation' does not mean 'a case'. Cover the reported 3-week hospital quarantines and how health authorities give preventive antibiotics to close contacts. Use Madagascar 2017 as the real-world example of an outbreak brought under control. Action framing modelled on the anaesthesia Short (57 views).
candidates.why_now: The 189–200 contact figure appears in almost every story, and 'quarantine' headlines (Reuters 'Dozens quarantined') create questions. Few pieces explain how the process works.

evidence.signal: Nearly 200 (189) people under medical observation in Irkutsk region
Several Irkutsk hospitals reportedly imposed a 3-week quarantine; no confirmed transmission

candidates.topic: Is plague airborne like COVID? Myth corrections circulating now: 'no cure', 'airborne', 'the Black Death is back'
candidates.angle: 'Is Plague Airborne Like COVID? 3 Plague Claims Checked'. Myth-busts aimed at beliefs viewers already hold, each correction credited to a named agency. Use 'not supported' rather than 'myth' for anything about the unconfirmed case. Never repeat bioweapon rumours.
candidates.why_now: Fear headlines ('We should be terrified', 'It's worse') are circulating. An attributed correction lands near our median (46/45) and fits the calm tone.

evidence.signal: 'Why a global outbreak of pneumonic plague is unlikely' (Oct 7)
Experts on risk level

candidates.topic: Why can't anyone confirm it's plague yet? How plague is diagnosed (culture, PCR, antigen tests) and why WHO needs the lab data
candidates.angle: 'Plague: Why Is It So Hard to Confirm?' Explain how labs identify Yersinia pestis and what 'pneumonia of unknown aetiology' means. Say what WHO has said it is missing (the causative agent, as of Oct 7). Neutral and procedural: no cover-up framing.
candidates.why_now: The story is now about the gap between 'suspected' and 'confirmed' (WHO 'not full picture', NYT 'What experts want to know'). Few creators explain diagnostics, so this is a clear gap.

evidence.signal: Van Kerkhove: WHO doesn't know the causative agent of the first death (Oct 7)
'Russian Plague Death: What We Know and Don't Know' (Oct 7)

candidates.topic: Bubonic vs septicemic vs pneumonic plague: the three forms of Yersinia pestis, and why only pneumonic passes between people
candidates.angle: 'Pneumonic vs Bubonic Plague: What's the Difference?' Comparison titles that name both sides. Cover how each starts (flea bite vs inhalation) and how bubonic can become pneumonic. Every table cell keeps the source's hedge.
candidates.why_now: Seen in 2 snapshots. Business Today and others are running 'pneumonic or bubonic' pieces. This is the evergreen anchor alongside the news.

evidence.signal: 'Pneumonic or bubonic: key differences' explainer
Official pneumonic plague explainer

candidates.topic: How labs that study plague keep it contained: biosafety levels, protective equipment and what happens after a possible lab exposure (Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute)
candidates.angle: 'How Do Plague Labs Keep It Contained?' Cover BSL-3 practice, airflow, PPE and post-exposure protocols as general procedure. Any detail of this incident, such as a reported broken test tube, appears only with a named source and is marked 'reported, not confirmed'. No blame on the worker.
candidates.why_now: Seen in 2 snapshots. PBS ('tight lid'), Time ('What worries experts') and The Conversation (microbiologist explainer) have pushed lab containment into the conversation. Plain biosafety explainers are still scarce.

evidence.signal: 'The death of a Russian plague researcher, explained by a microbiologist'
Reported (not officially confirmed) exposure to a broken test tube

candidates.topic: Is there a plague vaccine? Status of plague vaccines (none widely licensed in US/EU; live EV vaccine used in Russia/CIS; candidates in development)
candidates.angle: 'Is There a Vaccine for Plague?' Give each vaccine's status with exact scope: never move a finding about the killed USP vaccine onto the live EV vaccine (that was the 10-08 hold). Explain why antibiotics and contact tracing, not vaccines, are the main tools today.
keywords: is there a vaccine for plague
candidates.why_now: This is the natural next question after 'is it curable', and news pieces mostly skip it. Low competition, but the craft notes show a high scope-error risk, so it needs careful sourcing.

evidence.signal: Plague FAQ (Oct 5, 2026) covers prevention questions
Plague (disease) spike suggests broad curiosity

candidates.topic: Black Death vs 2026: what antibiotics, germ theory and public health changed
candidates.angle: 'Black Death vs Today: Why Plague Is Different Now'. Compare the 1300s with 2026 on the cause (unknown then, Y. pestis now), treatment (none vs antibiotics), and control (none vs tracing and isolation). Calm history, not doom. Avoid 'new Black Death' framing completely.
candidates.why_now: Smithsonian and others are invoking 'the disease behind the Black Death'. Long-form comparison fits our 'name both sides' formula.

evidence.signal: '…Sparking Concerns Over the Disease Behind the Black Death' (Oct 7)

candidates.topic: Madagascar 2017: how a large pneumonic plague outbreak was brought under control with contact tracing and preventive antibiotics
candidates.angle: 'How Did Madagascar Stop a Plague Outbreak?' Give WHO figures with denominators (notified vs confirmed cases) and the tools used. Say 'brought under control', not 'stopped'. Tie it to what Irkutsk-style monitoring aims for.
candidates.why_now: Seen in 2 snapshots (60 → 66). It gives a reassuring, evidence-based precedent while people wonder about outbreak risk.

evidence.signal: 'Should we be worried?' explainer referencing past outbreaks

candidates.topic: Pets and plague: cats, dogs, fleas and prevention in US plague areas
candidates.angle: 'Can Cats Get Plague? What Pet Owners in the West Should Know'. Cats can get sick and are a known source of US pneumonic cases (CDC). Cover flea control, with the caveat that dog flea products can be toxic to cats. See a vet for sick pets in plague areas.
candidates.why_now: US-angle follow-up to the AP 'plague never went away' piece. Pet questions are a practical, shareable niche with few creators covering it.

evidence.signal: Hiker/pet flea prevention context citing CDC

candidates.topic: Is plague becoming antibiotic resistant? Rare resistant isolates (e.g. Madagascar 1995) vs standard treatment efficacy
candidates.angle: Only with careful framing: 'Plague and Antibiotic Resistance: How Big Is the Risk?' Report only documented isolates, with their place and year, and do not generalise. Use this to counter the ACSH 'it's worse' headline calmly.
candidates.why_now: ACSH's 'The plague is back but it's not black. It's worse.' (Oct 8) may seed a resistance scare. This is a pre-emptive, evidence-led correction.

evidence.signal: 'The plague is back but it's not black. It's worse.' (Oct 8)

candidates.topic: 'Is the Russian plague a bioweapon?' (Trump: 'we don't think'; Rand Paul: could be 'weaponized')
candidates.angle: Do not produce. Guardrails forbid bioweapon, deliberate-release or cover-up speculation. Redirect the demand to the confirmed-vs-suspected decoder and the US-risk explainer.
candidates.why_now: WaPo, CNBC, ABC and NewsNation are running bioweapon-framed headlines. Search demand is high, but this is outside our guardrails.

evidence.signal: 'Rand Paul concerned Russian plague could be weaponized'

candidates.topic: 'We Should Be Terrified of What May Happen Next' fear framing (Popular Mechanics)
candidates.angle: Do not mirror it. This is fear-bait framing banned for titles, thumbnails and hooks. Use the calm myth-check candidate instead.
candidates.why_now: Doom headlines are circulating and invite copycat creators. We should stay out of that lane.

evidence.signal: 'A Russian Lab Worker Is Dead…We Should Be Terrified…' (Oct 5)
